title: The Palace of King David: Excavations at the Summit of the City of David, Preliminary Report of Seasons 2005-2007
author: Eilat Mazar
publisher: Shoham Academic Research and Publication, Jerusalem
allowedUseNotes: Copyrighted excavation report/monograph. Project stores its own summary of the reported findings and their interpretation only; no reproduction of plans, photographs, or the report's own text.
summary: Eilat Mazar's own preliminary excavation report for the 2005-2007 seasons at the northern summit of the City of David ridge, the site of what she calls the 'Large Stone Structure.' Mazar interprets this massive, poorly preserved wall complex — excavated over a stepped stone terrace system already known from Kathleen Kenyon's and Yigal Shiloh's earlier work — as part of a single large public building, and proposes, on the combined strength of the pottery recovered in its associated fills, its stratigraphic relationship to the older stepped structure, and her own reading of 2 Samuel 5:11 and 5:17 (David 'went down' from a residence at the summit to a stronghold), that it is plausibly the remains of David's palace, built with Phoenician assistance. This project cites Mazar as the named, checkable source of the maximalist identification (Large Stone Structure = a 10th-century BCE monumental building, read as a plausible palace) and does not adopt her identification as settled; see finkelstein-herzog-singer-avitz-ussishkin-2007 for the direct, named scholarly rebuttal on dating and structural-unity grounds.
confidenceNotes: Bibliographic details (publisher, 2009, ISBN 9789659029952, ~100pp, seasons 2005-2007) and the summary of Mazar's argument (Large Stone Structure interpreted as a single monumental building, tentatively dated 10th-9th century BCE, proposed as David's palace on combined stratigraphic/ceramic and biblical-textual grounds) are cross-corroborated across multiple independent secondary descriptions (BiblePlaces.com book notice, Biblical Archaeology Society articles, Wikipedia's Large Stone Structure article, and the Finkelstein et al. 2007 Tel Aviv rebuttal's own description of what it is responding to), not from direct page-by-page inspection of the print report itself, which does not appear to have an accessible full-text copy.
